content: Hop, also known as Hsp70-Hsp90 Organizing Protein, is a co-chaperone that facilitates the reversible interaction between the molecular chaperones Hsp70 and Hsp90. It is a member of a large family of co-chaperones that regulate and assist the function of major chaperones, particularly heat shock proteins. Among the co-chaperones of the Hsp70/Hsp90 complex, Hop is one of the most extensively studied. Initially discovered in yeast, homologs of Hop have been identified in humans, mice, rats, insects, plants, parasites, and viruses. The family of these proteins is referred to as STI1 (stress-inducible protein) and can be categorized into yeast, plant, and animal STI1 (Hop). The human Hop protein is encoded by a gene consisting of 14 exons. Structurally, STI proteins, including Hop, are characterized by the presence of nine tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) motifs, which are organized into three domains, each containing three TPR motifs. The TPR motif is a common structural feature in many proteins and is critical for mediating protein-protein interactions. Crystallographic studies have provided structural insights into the N-terminal TPR1 domain and the central TPR2A domain of Hop in complex with Hsp90 and Hsp70 ligand peptides, respectively. Hop, also known as STIP1 in humans, plays a pivotal role in transferring client proteins between Hsp70 and Hsp90. It is evolutionarily conserved across eukaryotes and is localized in both the nucleus and cytoplasm. In Drosophila, Hop exists as a monomeric protein composed of three TPR domains (TPR1, TPR2A, and TPR2B) and one aspartic acid-proline repeat domain (DP). The TPR domains interact with the C-terminal regions of Hsp70 and Hsp90, with TPR1 and TPR2B binding to Hsp70 and TPR2A preferentially binding to Hsp90. The transient and dynamic nature of chaperone function makes it challenging to fully characterize the intermediate structures of the heat shock machinery. The primary function of Hop is to link Hsp70 and Hsp90, but recent studies suggest that it also modulates the chaperone activities of these proteins and may interact with other chaperones and proteins. Beyond its role in the Hsp70/Hsp90 chaperone machinery, Hop appears to participate in other protein complexes, such as the signal transduction complex EcR/USP and the Hepatitis B virus reverse transcriptase complex, which facilitates viral replication. Additionally, Hop acts as a receptor for prion proteins. It is found in various cellular regions and shuttles between the cytoplasm and nucleus. In Drosophila, Hop has been identified as an integral component of the pre-RISC complex involved in RNA interference pathways for siRNAs. In the Piwi-interacting RNA (piRNA) pathway, which represses transposable elements (transposons), Hop interacts with Piwi. In the absence of Hop, transposons become derepressed, leading to significant genomic instability and infertility. Human Hop (STIP1) has been shown to interact with the prion protein PRNP and the cytosolic heat shock protein Hsp90α (member A1).
